store.0: I'm a Computer Science major, and I'm in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is really packed, but it's a good kind of busy. I'm finally taking the higher-level courses that seemed so far away when I was a freshman. It's surreal to be at this stage. It feels like just yesterday I was in an intro class learning about simple data structures, but now I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even basics of quantum computing. It's exciting to see how far I've come!

store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving. For example, how do we optimize pathfinding in large networks, or what's the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity? These kinds of problems are super fascinating to me. In class, we've been diving into everything from dynamic programming approaches to approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It really messes with your head sometimes, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great; she has a knack for explaining these dizzying concepts in a really intuitive manner. She'll put up a problem on the board—something you'd think is impossible to solve in polynomial time—and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain's buzzing.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second hardest. It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is definitely an adventure. We have to collaborate with folks who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas of what the final product should look like. But that's also the beauty of it, right? In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle everything from concurrency issues to node failures gracefully. It's nerve-wracking at times—like last week, I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we got that fixed and everything ran smoothly, it was this huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. To be honest, I've always been a gamer at heart, so this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.

store.8: I also have an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which I might have regretted signing up for at first, but now I actually enjoy. It sounds cutting-edge, right? Initially, it was intimidating, but the professor's approach is to make it more about conceptual understanding than pure math. Of course, there is math—like linear algebra out the wazoo—but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers or anything, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.

store.10: I'm also taking a Capstone Project course, which is basically the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It sounds fancy, but it essentially means reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could theoretically use to see real-time alerts. It's definitely pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major: database management, building an API, front-end interface, plus the ML pipeline. Because it's a real, end-to-end solution, we're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.

store.12: I'm also taking a Philosophy of Mind course, which is my last required non-CS elective. I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how that might apply to artificial intelligence. It's a smaller class, so we do a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. Sometimes it's nice to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas. This course also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia—like the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was such a trip to research. I think bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for that perspective.

store.14: I'm juggling a typical college schedule. Mondays and Wednesdays are packed. I start at 9:30 am with Advanced Algorithms, then I've got a short break to refuel before heading to my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00. After lunch, I've got the Capstone meeting, which can be all over the place—sometimes it's a lecture, sometimes it's lab work, sometimes it's project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with just Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. Philosophy of Mind is on Thursday evenings, which can be brutal if I'm tired from the rest of the day. But hey, it's senior year, and I gotta push through. Fridays are open, with no scheduled classes, but inevitably I'm working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab that's focusing on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload.

store.16: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. Capstone alone can eat up a solid ten hours a week—more if you run into a big bug or if your model's not training properly. Then the Distributed Systems project is another black hole for time. My group tries to meet at least twice a week. We also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to keep each other updated. Coordinating five different people's schedules is a mini-nightmare. Still, as stressful as it can be, it's also exciting. This is going to be among my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic, purely about learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment.

store.18: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night—once in a while you just can't avoid it, especially if something's due the next day and you're stuck debugging. But it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. I guess that's the biggest takeaway: after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.

store.20: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's pretty cool to be part of that. As a freshman, I didn't see myself going down the research route. I was into coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't think of research as 'my thing.' However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed my ability to bridge technical coding with user experience. She told me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating. But I took the leap, and it turned out to be a great decision.

store.25: I've always been fascinated by the idea of exploring new places, and that's something I've tried to do whenever my schedule allows. Since I'm a fourth-year Computer Science major, I have to be pretty strategic about planning my trips—between classes, research, campus clubs, and even everyday stuff like heading to the gym or working on group projects, my calendar gets ridiculously cramped. But I've managed to squeeze in some adventures that have given me some of my favorite memories so far.
store.26: I took a sailing trip off the coast of Maine with a friend before my sophomore year. We spent a week exploring the coastal towns of New England. It was breathtaking. We'd wake up early, feel the crisp salt air on our faces, and watch the sunrise over the water. We'd sail past islands dotted with pine trees and have breakfast on the deck, discussing our routes for the day. We had a local instructor who taught us about navigation using modern technology and old-school methods with star charts. It was thrilling to disconnect from my coding mindset and focus on the wind, tide charts, and the synergy of the boat with nature. And I'll never forget the fresh lobster rolls we got at a small dockside shack – still the best lobster I've ever had.
store.27: I saved up money from a summer internship to go to Japan during my junior year's winter break. I had read about Japan's blend of modern technology and traditional culture, and it seemed like a dream destination for a computer science student who also loves discovering local history. I went to Tokyo first, because it's the tech hub. Walking around Akihabara, seeing the bustling arcades, and dropping by electronics stores was like a futuristic wonderland. I tried to pick up some Japanese phrases before the trip—mostly just greetings and basic directions. It was helpful, but I still ended up pointing at menus a bunch of times while ordering ramen. The food was so good, though. Tokyo's also where I saw that crazy intersection in Shibuya—so many people crossing at once, yet it somehow felt orderly. After a few days there, I headed to Kyoto, which was the total opposite vibe—very calm and historical. I visited a number of shrines and temples, and even caught a glimpse of geishas quietly walking down a side street near Gion. It was surreal. I remember writing in my journal that being in Kyoto felt like stepping back into an older era, where craftsmanship and tradition take center stage. That sense of stillness and reverence left a big impression on me.
store.28: I took a family vacation to Europe last summer. We flew into London and spent a few days exploring the city. We visited the Tower of London, the British Museum, and rode on the London Eye. My sister is really into history, so she was excited to see all the old artifacts and crown jewels. We also went to see a musical in the West End, which was The Phantom of the Opera. After London, we took a train to Paris. It was my first time in France, and I barely remembered any French phrases beyond "bonjour" and "merci." However, it was easy to get around, and the city is so beautiful. My favorite spot was the area around the Seine River near Notre-Dame, where we could stroll and enjoy the scenery. It was a really relaxing experience, especially compared to the hustle of London. My dad loves art, so we spent a whole day at the Louvre, but even that didn't feel like enough time. You could easily spend a week there without seeing everything.
store.29: I've also done some smaller getaways with my roommates. We'd drive out to a state park or a nearby beach town on weekends. It was always fun packing up the car with snacks, fishing rods(since one of my roommates is into fishing), and turning up the music. We'd set up a quick campsite or rent a small cabin for the night. One time, we found ourselves in a remote area with horrible cellphone reception, which initially drove us crazy since we couldn't check social media or quickly Google stuff. However, by the end of that weekend, we realized it was exactly what we needed: a digital detox. We ended up hiking around, telling stories, and just enjoying nature. That trip reminded me how necessary it is to occasionally step away from my laptop and, ironically, it recharged me for the programming tasks waiting for me back at campus.
store.30: I'm planning a big trip before I graduate. I've been eyeing some internships in Silicon Valley for next summer, so if that pans out, I might spend a couple of weeks exploring the West Coast. I've heard great things about Portland, Seattle, and Vancouver – everyone always praises the coffee, craft beer, and beautiful scenery. If I line things up just right, I could do a road trip through Washington and Oregon after my internship ends, maybe with a friend or two who'll also be interning in the Bay Area. It would be awesome to discover the coastal highways, the Redwood forests, and those hidden beaches I keep seeing in photos. That might be my last chance to have a big chunk of free time before the post-grad grind starts.
store.31: I'd love to travel with my dog one day. I have a Golden Retriever named Archie who's super energetic. One time, my family considered taking him on a road trip, but Archie hates being cooped up in a car for too long—he gets fidgety and starts pawing at the windows. So we decided to leave him with my uncle for that trip. Still, I dream of traveling in an RV or camper van, bringing Archie along for hikes and beach runs. It'd be a different type of adventure, but definitely one that'd make for some amazing memories.
store.32: Travel to me isn't just about ticking places off a bucket list. Of course, it's cool to say I've been to different countries or states, but I really value the experiences that come from stepping outside my usual environment. I feel like each locale has taught me something – Japan gave me a sense of reverence for tradition and efficiency, Maine reminded me how timeless and beautiful nature can be, and Europe opened my eyes to the depth of art and culture spanning centuries. Even short trips nearby campus help me unwind and discover hidden gems in my own area. I love collecting postcards along the way, too – every time I look at them, I'm reminded that there's a big, wide world beyond my bedroom. And the more I see, the more inspired I am, not just for personal enjoyment, but also for the creative problem-solving that goes into my coding projects and research ideas. There's something about experiencing new places that heightens my curiosity and makes me want to explore fresh angles in everything I do.
store.33: Traveling has become one of my passions that I'll keep nurturing even after graduation. I'm excited to see where my future career in computer science will lead me – I hope to land a job that allows some remote work days or flexible scheduling, so I can keep exploring. Whether it's a weekend trip to a mountain range a few hours away or a flight to a completely different continent, I'm all in. If I ever get the chance to combine my love of coding with my love of travel – like working abroad for a stint or collaborating on an international project – I'd jump at the chance. For now, I'm just enjoying planning the next journey in my head whenever I need a mental break from debugging code. It keeps me motivated, and it's a huge part of why I'm super pumped for the next phase of my life.
